uniequip_002_shu:
'Hey, Tianshi Shu, there are some things I just don't get no matter how much I think them over, and I thought you could help teach me.'
Shu raises her head, the Tianshi apparatus that was hovering before her gracefully collapsing into a cube before falling back into her palm. Her young visitor's arms and legs were hooked into the branches of a tree, her hands grasping some brilliant red fruit, her sharp eyes quite unlike her youthful figure hanging upside-down, and staring at the apparatus in Shu's hand.
Shu laughs, holding the apparatus tight, and says: 'It's rare to see you in the fields. Do you not have schoolwork to mark?'
'That group of layabouts? Let someone else who cares take charge of that lot!' The child wipes the fruit with her sleeve, gobbling down a bite, its sweet scent clear even from two or three zhang away. 'What about you? You're hardly an ordinary person yourself, so what are you doing mucking about with a Tianshi apparatus for? Can't you decide how good the harvest will be with a point of your finger and a glance of your eye?'
'And what if I don't have this mystical power you speak of? What if I have simply seen enough to know if the weather will change, or if the seeds will successfully become crops?'
'You do, though! Look, don't play dumb, I'm asking you seriously here.'
Shu stoops down towards the field, her cloud-like tail slowly sweeping across the chilly crop ridges. These plants had just passed the seedling stage, and would soon join the sprouts that had been brought onto the agricultural plate alongside their fields, gleaming in the burning embers of the summer evening.
'Springtime drizzles wake the seeds, grain buds dance in summer's heat. Autumn gifts the crops their gold, but they can't stand winter's cold.' She recites this softly, as if reminiscing on the prior night's dream. 'One person's strength alone could not order the myriad grains everlasting. But before I was I, before Shu was Shu, there was already someone who had achieved half of what was dictated in this song of the jieqi solar terms.
'A thousand years hence, those that came after her created this Tianshi apparatus. It can take on six forms, knows how seeds will develop, can share data between different plates, and can direct Sky Poles.' The little green cube floats above Shu's palm once more. 'Although mine is somewhat different, its functions are still interlinked: whether it is the song of the jieqi or a Tianshi apparatus, they are but manifestations of the power of the architecture of time.'
'Pah.' A fruit pit leaps into the heavens like a signal flare, its furious rise startling some featherbeasts roosting in the tree, only landing far away a long while later. 'Forget I ever asked. Breaking out some old Shennong cliche again to avoid the question, how boring.'
The child leaps down from the tree, walking off along a small path without another look. As if coming to a sudden realization, Shu lightly claps her hands.
'Could it be that the reason you came... is that you don't know how to use an apparatus? How about I go ask He Sheng to teach you...'
'Don't talk rubbish!'
uniequip_003_shu:
Shu walked into that "heart," which had long lain still.
Building this enormous machine had cost her and her sisters no small effort, but in the end it did not become the last-resort move in that chess player's calculations for the worst-case scenario. Now it seemed to have become a real heart, one end connected to this land that had been tilled for a thousand years, the other to a faint consciousness in a mausoleum a thousand miles away. Shu could feel that connection.
Shu wanted this heart to keep growing and beating. It was not only that the people working here needed it; she had a strong premonition, or perhaps it was only her own wishful thinking, that her "elder brother" would someday need it too.
She carefully poured her own power into the "heart," and afterward, she had a dream brimming with the fragrance of rice blossoms.
Insects chirped softly, and she heard the sounds of all things: the rustle of tender rice leaves growing, the muffled sound of roots driving into the soil, even the gathering of rain clouds, as if right by her ear.
The rain soon came pouring down. A blurry figure carrying a hoe came over, took her hand, and led her to dig a channel together, just as when it had first taught her. The water pooled in the field drained away, yet the rain still scattered the seeds in disarray. Fortunately, the remaining seeds struggled to put down tender yet strong roots and sprout new shoots.
But soon a wind swept through, hurling down hailstones nearly the size of fists; the frail seedlings were torn out by the roots and flung back into the soil. In a gale so fierce she could not open her eyes, someone handed her a bolt of cloth. She spread the cloth to shelter the tottering seedlings and reinforced the trellis with branches, toiling tirelessly. At last the wind stopped. When she looked up, the seedlings were already blooming with fragrant rice flowers. The small white blossoms filled her heart with deep joy, but the beating of insect wings ominously sounded.
A plague of insects descended, blotting out the sky, and in her nearly pitch-black vision Shu could see only a figure walking ahead of her. A flame rose beside that person, driving back the endlessly surging swarm. The fire burned ever fiercer, until the blackness before her eyes turned crimson.
Shu looked at the scattered seedlings and, still carrying her hoe, tended them with care, weeding, watering, fertilizing. Day after day, year after year, through wind, frost, rain and snow, drought, flood, pests and hail, time flowed past the woman's feet like a river. Her hair grew longer and longer, merging into the azure of the river; the hem of her skirt was stained green by grass and brown by soil. She repeated this labor, until a muffled voice sounded from within the earth.
"You are tired."
"You rarely appear in anyone's dreams, and now that you do, you have nothing to say, so you take the shapes of all these calamities to frighten people instead?"
"I merely wished to tell you that, at this point, these efforts are nothing but futile."
"When you went off alone to wrestle with that fate of such faint hope, did I ever once call your efforts futile?"
The muffled voice in the earth wanted to say more, but Shu merely turned and brushed her hand over the green rice seedlings. As the rice blossoms fell, two curious wine cups had appeared beside her. The colors of the sky shifted like ink wash, the food in the metal lunchbox on the stone beside her was still steaming, and a few medicinal herbs in the back basket bore fresh dew. A clear breeze blew past like silk, the plants made sounds like music, and the rice swayed and rustled as if in harmony; then suddenly the wind grew as forceful as fists and kicks, twisting and turning a hundred times over, until everything fell, along with the fine raindrops from the sky, into the wine cups.
"This is the wine my elder sister brewed this year. It was made from the dreams of a few of us, a shared dream."
No one spoke, but the other cup slowly vanished, as if someone had drained it. He could savor the fragrance of the dreams in the wine, and he knew what this cup meant. The taste of hope is always a little more fragrant.
"I didn't give you that handful of seeds just so you could end up with nothing but 'a life for a life.' I'm still waiting for that harvest season. It would be best if the whole family could enjoy it together, without a single one missing...
"That ought to be a good season."
